title: English for Work & Life
tagline: Write clear emails, speak with confidence, ace interviews and presentations, and use plain English that gets results.

superpower.name: Clear Voice
superpower.description: Writes and speaks clearly: better interviews, deals and friendships.

syllabus: Week 1: Plain English: short, clear, active
Week 2: Emails and messages that get answers
Week 3: Speaking, presenting and small talk
Week 4: CVs, cover letters and interviews

weeks.title: Plain English
weeks.objective: Write so anyone understands you the first time.

slides.title: Short Words, Short Sentences
slides.body: Clear writing respects the reader's time. Use everyday words, keep sentences to about 15 to 20 words, and put the main point first.
bullets: 'Use' not 'utilise'; 'help' not 'facilitate'; 'start' not 'commence'
One idea per sentence
Main point first, details after
Cut words that add nothing: 'in order to' becomes 'to'
slides.example:
Before: 'We would like to take this opportunity to inform you that your application has been successfully processed.'
After: 'Your application is approved.'
slides.takeaway: If a 12-year-old can understand it, your boss will love it.

slides.title: Active Voice
slides.body: In active sentences, the person doing the action comes first. They're shorter, clearer and show who's responsible.
bullets: Passive: 'The report was finished by Sara.' Active: 'Sara finished the report.'
Passive hides who did it: 'Mistakes were made.'
Use active voice by default; passive only when the doer doesn't matter
slides.takeaway: Name who does what, and your writing gets stronger.

lab.title: Rewrite Lab
lab.brief: Rewrite five long, formal paragraphs in plain English, cutting each by at least a third.
lab.deliverable: Before and after versions with word counts.
lab.proTip: Read it aloud: if you run out of breath, the sentence is too long.

caseStudy.scenario: Your manager says your report is 'hard to follow'. What's the best first fix?

options.text: Add more technical words to sound expert.
Put the main conclusion first, shorten sentences and use headings.
options.explanation: Structure and plain language fix most 'hard to follow' writing.

quiz.question: Which sentence is active?
options: The car was washed by Ali.

weeks.title: Emails and Messages
weeks.objective: Write emails and messages that get quick, useful replies.

slides.title: The Perfect Work Email
slides.body: Busy people read the subject line and the first two lines. Make those count.
bullets: Subject line says what you need: 'Approval needed: Q3 budget by Thursday'
First line: the request or the point
Then context, in short paragraphs or bullets
End with the next step and the deadline
slides.example:
Subject: Can you approve the venue deposit by Thursday?
Hi Omar,
Could you approve the AED 5,000 deposit for the launch venue by Thursday? The venue holds the date until Friday.
Quote attached. Happy to call if easier.
Thanks,
Lina
slides.takeaway: Ask clearly, give a deadline, keep it short.

slides.title: Tone Across Cultures
slides.body: Dubai workplaces mix dozens of nationalities. Polite, warm and direct works almost everywhere.
bullets: Greet by name; 'Hi' or 'Dear' depending on formality
Please and thank you, always
Avoid sarcasm and jokes that may not translate
On WhatsApp for work: short, polite, and still professional
slides.takeaway: Be kind and clear: it translates into every culture.

lab.title: Email Lab
lab.brief: Write three emails: a request, a polite follow-up and a complaint, each under 120 words.
lab.proTip: Write the subject line last: once you know your point.

caseStudy.scenario: A colleague hasn't replied to your request for a week. What's best?

options.text: Send an angry email copying their boss.
Send a short, friendly follow-up with the request and deadline in the first line.
options.explanation: A polite, clear nudge usually works.

quiz.question: What should the first line of a work email contain?

weeks.title: Speaking and Presenting
weeks.objective: Speak confidently in meetings, presentations and everyday conversation.

slides.title: Presenting With Confidence
slides.body: Great presentations have one clear message, a simple structure and a speaker who has practised.
bullets: Structure: tell them what you'll say, say it, then sum it up
One idea per slide, few words, big visuals
Practise out loud three times
Look at people, pause, and slow down
slides.takeaway: Nerves are normal: preparation turns them into energy.

slides.title: Small Talk and Listening
slides.body: Relationships start with small talk. Ask open questions, listen, and remember details.
bullets: Open questions: 'What brought you to Dubai?' rather than 'Do you like Dubai?'
Listen more than you speak
Remember names and use them
Safe topics: travel, food, work, sport; avoid politics and religion at first
slides.takeaway: People remember how you made them feel, not what you said.

lab.title: Presentation Lab
lab.brief: Give a 3-minute talk on something you know well, with three slides, and ask a friend for feedback.
lab.deliverable: Your slides and the feedback notes.
lab.proTip: Record yourself once: you'll spot the filler words.

caseStudy.scenario: You're asked to present tomorrow and you feel very nervous. What helps most?

options.text: Write every word on the slides and read them.
Prepare one clear message, practise out loud, and keep slides simple.
Speak as fast as possible to finish quickly.
options.explanation: Rushing makes it harder to follow.

quiz.question: An open question is:
options: What do you enjoy about your work?

weeks.title: CVs and Interviews
weeks.objective: Win interviews with a strong CV and confident answers.

slides.title: A CV That Gets Read
slides.body: Recruiters scan a CV in seconds. Lead with results, keep it to one or two pages, and match it to the job.
bullets: Start with a 2 to 3 line summary
Achievements with numbers: 'cut delivery time by 20%'
Use the job advert's key words
Clean layout; no photo needed unless asked
slides.example:
Weak: 'Responsible for social media.'
Strong: 'Grew Instagram followers from 2,000 to 15,000 in 6 months, raising online orders by 30%.'
slides.takeaway: Show what you achieved, not just what you did.

slides.title: Interview Answers With STAR
slides.body: Behavioural questions ('Tell me about a time…') are answered best with STAR.
bullets: Situation: the background
Task: what you had to do
Action: what you did
Result: what happened, with numbers if possible

lab.title: Interview Lab
lab.brief: Rewrite your CV with achievement bullets, then answer three common questions using STAR.
lab.deliverable: A one-page CV and three STAR answers.
lab.proTip: Prepare 5 stories that can answer most questions.

caseStudy.scenario: An interviewer asks: 'Tell me about a time you solved a problem.' The best answer:

options.text: A STAR story: the situation, your task, your actions and the measurable result.

options.explanation: Everyone has problems; show how you handle them.

questions.question: A work email should end with:
'Mistakes were made' is:
questions.explanation: Passive: it hides who did it.

questions.question: An open question begins with:
questions.explanation: What, how, why invite fuller answers.
